Date: 2026-07-28
Time: 16:00 - 16:54 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jae Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (BrightScale CTO), Ruben Ortiz (BrightScale Lead ML Eng), Lina Park (BrightScale Infra), Derek Cole (BrightScale Procurement)
summary: Deep dive on throughput tuning for BrightScale's inference workloads. Covered continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, batch timeout, max tokens per request), KV cache impacts, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run a 1-day pilot with representative traces; Redwood to share tuning guide, scheduler examples, and pricing/benchmarks for Dedicated tier.
transcript:
[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep to 50 minutes, lots to cover on tuning throughput for your deployment.
[00:08] Maya Thompson: Thanks, Ava, yeah goal is to get predictible token throughput cost and keep tail latency below 150ms for our chat product.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Cool, quick intros? I'll focus on runtime knobs.
[00:22] Ruben Ortiz: Ruben - lead ML eng, we run a custom gpt-ish model (34B) quantized to 4-bit, inference on DGX hosts on prem.
[00:32] Jae Kim: Jae here, I'll help with config examples and follow-ups.
[00:37] Lina Park: Lina infra, net and VPC peering for pilot.
[00:41] Derek Cole: Derek procurement - just listening for licensing / pricing notes.
[00:46] Samir Patel: Great. High level first: three levers for throughput — batching behavior (continuous batching), scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, batch timeout / max_wait_ms), and model-side limits (max tokens / seq length). We'll also touch KV cache and quantization.
[01:05] Ruben Ortiz: Walk me through continuous batching again — we saw spikes but sometimes batch sizes stay tiny.
[01:10] Samir Patel: Sure. The runtime uses continuous batching — it keeps an inflight batch slot open for a short window while aggregating requests. There are two important parameters: batch_timeout (how long to wait for more requests) and max_num_seqs (maximum concurrent sequences per GPU/inference instance). If your request arrival rate is bursty, increasing batch_timeout to 8-12ms can increase batch size but adds tail latency.
[01:35] Maya Thompson: For us tail latency SLA is 150ms, average is fine to be higher but tail not. So we can't add too much timeout.
[01:42] Samir Patel: Understood. Another approach is to increase max_num_seqs and use multiple sequence packing: if your average prompt length is short (<=50 tokens) you can pack multiple sequences into a single batch to improve utilization without increasing per-request latency. We'll need to tune max_seq_len and padding behavior.
[02:05] Ruben Ortiz: Our user prompts vary a lot, 30-400 tokens. Does packing still help?
[02:11] Samir Patel: Packing helps for the short-request percent. We often recommend analyzing token distribution and using a two-tier scheduler: keep a low batch_timeout for latency-sensitive small-requests and have a background batcher for large/off-peak workloads — that's where continuous batching + prioritized scheduling helps.
[02:31] Jae Kim: (mild crosstalk) Also consider max_tokens_per_request caps — you can reject or redirect long requests to a lower-cost model variant to protect latency.
[02:41] Lina Park: Any network implications with VPC / on-prem that will affect batching?
[02:45] Samir Patel: Yes: egress latency and jitter matter. If your VPC peering or private link has 5-10ms variance, batcher sees arrival jitter which reduces effective batch sizes. For on-prem, colocating request ingress with the GPU hosts or using an edge aggregator helps.
[03:02] Maya Thompson: We have an edge tier that terminates TLS in the DMZ and then tunnels to on-prem inference. Could that introduce jitter?
[03:08] Samir Patel: Potentially. For the pilot, we recommend measuring tail-to-tail request latency (edge -> inference host). If jitter is significant, increase worker threads on the ingress to smooth bursts and set batch_timeout to compensate by a small amount (2-6ms).
[03:26] Ruben Ortiz: You mentioned scheduler knobs — which ones should we tune first?
[03:30] Samir Patel: Priorities: 1) max_num_seqs per instance, 2) batch_timeout (ms), 3) max_active_batches, 4) seq_packing_enabled, 5) priority queues for latency classes. Start with increasing max_num_seqs from default 8 to 12-16 for your 34B model if GPU memory allows. That increases concurrency. Then tune batch_timeout in 2ms steps while watching tail latency.
[03:52] Jae Kim: Quick note: when upping max_num_seqs you may need to adjust KV cache allocation to avoid thrashing.
[03:58] Ruben Ortiz: KV cache thrash? We rely on per-request KV caches but not persistent across requests.
[04:04] Samir Patel: Right, ephemeral KV cache is typical and is cleared per request. Persistent KV (prefix caching) gives big wins for repeated context but uses memory. With higher concurrency, the runtime accounts for KV memory per sequence; if you overcommit max_num_seqs the allocator will evict or spill, increasing CPU/GPU copies and hurting throughput.
[04:24] Maya Thompson: How big is KV per sequence for 34B? Rough number?
[04:28] Samir Patel: Roughly 2-3GB of KV per 1k tokens at int8/4-bit quantization might be less, but depends on full attention state. For 34B and long histories, plan memory budget conservatively — we can run probes to measure exact.
[04:46] Ruben Ortiz: Our average history is 350 tokens per conversation.
[04:49] Samir Patel: That helps — you won't hit extreme KV sizes. But with many concurrent seqs, it adds up.
[04:55] Derek Cole: On pricing, does Dedicated pricing change with higher concurrency?
[04:59] Ava Chen: Pricing tiers are based on reserved capacity and usage; efficiency gains reduce per-token cost, but committed slots are billed. We'll send spreadsheet showing per-GPU throughput vs cost.
[05:10] Maya Thompson: On quantization — we already use 4-bit. Any runtime knobs specific to quantized models?
[05:15] Samir Patel: Yes, quantized models can run faster but are more sensitive to kernel selection and sequence length. Key knobs: enable quant-kernel-preference in the runtime so it picks fused kernels for 4-bit; set small-batch-kernel-threshold to prefer different kernels for tiny batches, and ensure we have FP32 fallback for rare ops.
[05:36] Jae Kim: We sometimes saw weird hallucinations when mixing quantized kernels — so ensure model validation when changing kernel prefs.
[05:41] Samir Patel: Absolutely. We'll provide an eval checklist.
[05:44] Ruben Ortiz: About max_num_seqs — is it per GPU or per worker process?
[05:48] Samir Patel: It's per worker process. Our default deployment runs 2 workers per GPU for isolation; you can run 1 worker per GPU to increase memory headroom and then raise max_num_seqs, or keep 2 workers and tune per-worker concurrency. There's a tradeoff: more workers gives isolation but reduces memory per worker.
[06:06] Lina Park: Any recommended starting values for our DGX A100-ish hosts?
[06:10] Samir Patel: For A100 80GB with 34B quantized, start with worker_count=1 per GPU, max_num_seqs=12, batch_timeout=4ms, seq_packing_enabled=true, small_batch_kernel_threshold=4. Then run a ramp test: linear increase in qps while letting the scheduler adapt.
[06:29] Maya Thompson: Ramp test — what telemetry should we watch?
[06:32] Samir Patel: Token throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU util, memory headroom, KV cache eviction rate, and kernel fallback events. Redwood Console exposes these; we'll share the dashboard widget.
[06:45] Ruben Ortiz: Kernel fallback events?
[06:47] Samir Patel: If a preferred fused kernel isn't available for a given seq length / batch size, the runtime falls back to a slower kernel — that's a perf cliff indicator.
[06:58] Jae Kim: We'll also capture per-token compute ms to see where hot spots are.
[07:02] Maya Thompson: Any risk with turning on seq_packing? Padding waste?
[07:06] Samir Patel: Padding is the tradeoff. Packed sequences reduce overhead but can increase padding tokens if lengths mismatch. Use a bucketing strategy: group by length ranges to reduce padding. Redwood supports automatic bucketing in the batcher.
[07:19] Ruben Ortiz: Good. VPC specifics — for the pilot we want to run in our test VPC but keep control plane with Redwood. Any gotchas?
[07:27] Samir Patel: Two main items: network egress and keys. Ensure KMS connectivity and restricted egress for model downloads. Also TLS termination points — if you terminate at the edge, make sure keepalive and connection pooling to inference hosts is enabled to avoid extra TCP handshake latency.
[07:45] Lina Park: We'll confirm firewall rules, may need to open some ephemeral ports.
[07:49] Samir Patel: We'll provide a minimal port list.
[07:52] Ruben Ortiz: How should we handle long requests — > 1024 tokens — in terms of scheduler?
[07:56] Samir Patel: Two strategies: 1) set a per-request token limit and redirect over-limit requests to a background queue / lower-priority worker; 2) split long requests server-side into streamed chunks with KV cache reuse, but that requires model behavior awareness. For chat it's often better to enforce a 2k token cap and guide users to summarize.
[08:16] Maya Thompson: We don't want user-facing truncation. Splitting with KV reuse — is that robust?
[08:20] Samir Patel: It's robust if you can deterministically stitch outputs and maintain context. The runtime supports streaming generation with KV reuse between chunks; we can demo.
[08:28] Derek Cole: From procurement standpoint, pilot obligations?
[08:31] Ava Chen: Pilot is free for 1 day of compute as a benchmark; if BrightScale moves to Dedicated we'll roll pilot credits into contract. We'll follow up with terms.
[08:39] Maya Thompson: Ok. Can you walk through a concrete config example?
[08:43] Jae Kim: (shares screen) Here's a sample scheduler block: max_num_seqs=12; batch_timeout_ms=4; max_active_batches=64; seq_packing=true; bucket_ranges=[0-64,65-256,257-1024]; small_batch_kernel_threshold=4.
[09:05] Samir Patel: Right, and for the worker: worker_count=1 per GPU, prefetch_requests=16, affinity=0. Set monitor thresholds to raise autoscaling signals when p95>120ms.
[09:20] Ruben Ortiz: Did you say prefetch_requests=16? That could starve GPU?
[09:24] Samir Patel: Prefetch is about pipeline depth on the CPU side; 16 is fine for A100 but reduce if you see CPU bottlenecks. We'll include guidance per CPU/GPU ratio.
[09:35] Maya Thompson: On autoscaling — we prefer predictable throughput with reserved Dedicated capacity, not aggressive autoscaling.
[09:42] Ava Chen: Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools; autoscaling config is soft and can be disabled for strict predictability.
[09:48] Ruben Ortiz: What about warm vs cold model load times — quantized model load can be like 60s?
[09:53] Samir Patel: Model load depends on quant format and whether kernel caches are primed. Warm-up scripts that run a few short prompts prime kernels and KV structures; we recommend a 30-90s warm-up after deploy. We'll provide a warm-up job example.
[10:07] Maya Thompson: If we do rolling deploys, any guidance to avoid tail latency spikes?
[10:12] Samir Patel: Canary with traffic mirroring helps; Redwood supports canary weights and automatic fallback if latency rises. Also stagger worker restarts so not all workers on a GPU reload simultaneously.
[10:23] Jae Kim: Add health probes that check p95 latency before marking instance READY.
[10:28] Lina Park: Regarding KV cache persistence, any disk-backed options?
[10:32] Samir Patel: Not for hot KV — it's in GPU memory. There are experimental on-device persistence options that keep KV across restarts but they're not generally available. For now rely on warm-up and prefix caching.
[10:45] Ruben Ortiz: We have around 300 concurrent users at peak leading to ~120 QPS, each average 120 tokens. Any ballpark on tokens/sec per A100?
[10:55] Samir Patel: Ballpark: for 34B quantized 4-bit on A100-80GB you might see ~1200-2000 tokens/sec per GPU depending on packing and kernel fusion. With packing and good scheduler you'll increase effective tokens/sec. We'll benchmark with your traces.
[11:12] Maya Thompson: Sounds promising. Anything else on quantization tradeoffs?
[11:15] Samir Patel: Lower-bit quant improves throughput but can slightly affect perplexity; always validate quality with your eval set. Also watch for outlier tokens where fallback to FP32 occurs.
[11:25] Ruben Ortiz: We'll provide eval prompts.
[11:28] Samir Patel: Great. For the pilot, suggested checklist: 1) provide traces and token distribution; 2) provide VPC peering details; 3) provision test GPUs in your VPC or allow Redwood to run on dedicated infra in your region; 4) choose representative model and quant config.
[11:48] Ava Chen: I'll email that checklist and the benchmark sheet.
[11:52] Derek Cole: Is there any compliance paperwork needed for the pilot?
[11:55] Ava Chen: For a short pilot, basic NDA and data handling notes suffice; for Private deployments we'll go through SOC2/ISO paperwork.
[12:03] Maya Thompson: Ok let's talk about fallback strategies if a GPU node gets saturated.
[12:07] Samir Patel: Runtime can route to compatible model variants or region fallback. You can configure a soft limit where if p95 exceeds threshold, new requests go to a smaller model for best-effort completion. This prevents queue buildup.
[12:22] Ruben Ortiz: Will switching models affect token accounting?
[12:25] Ava Chen: Yes, we account per-model per-token; rib pricing sheet will show variance. We'll include example cost delta.
[12:33] Lina Park: Any specific logs we need to collect on our side for debugging?
[12:37] Samir Patel: Request arrival timestamps, sizes, chosen model variant, kernel selection events, KV eviction events, worker memory usage. We'll provide a log schema.
[12:49] Maya Thompson: Alright — next steps?
[12:51] Ava Chen: Recap: Redwood to send tuning guide, benchmark spreadsheet, scheduler example config, and port/KMS checklist. BrightScale to share traces and confirm VPC details. Schedule pilot for week of Aug 10.
[12:59] Ruben Ortiz: Sounds good.
[13:02] Derek Cole: Thanks team.
[13:04] Ava Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up.
[13:08] (meeting ends)
